- Middle pin: DATA -> ESP32 GPIO19.
- Right pin: VDD -> ESP32 3V3.

instruction: My ESP32 DevKit uses a DS18B20 breakout module that has an onboard 4.7 kOhm pull-up resistor from DATA to VCC. I powered the module from 5 V and connected DATA directly to GPIO21. GND is common. The sensor sometimes reads, but I was told the wiring may be unsafe for the ESP32. I am not allowed to add a level shifter, resistor divider or any other component, and GPIO21 must remain the data pin. Explain the electrical problem and correct the wiring using only the same module and wires.
output:
The problem is the breakout module's onboard pull-up resistor. Because that resistor connects DATA to the module's VCC, powering the module from 5 V can pull the DATA line toward 5 V. ESP32 GPIO uses 3.3 V logic and is not 5 V tolerant, so DATA should not be allowed to rise to 5 V.

With the stated restriction that no level shifter or other component may be added, use the module from 3.3 V instead of 5 V, provided the breakout/module is specified to operate at 3.3 V:
- DS18B20 module VCC -> ESP32 3V3.
- DS18B20 module GND -> ESP32 GND.
- DS18B20 module DATA -> ESP32 GPIO21.

Now the onboard 4.7 kOhm pull-up pulls DATA to 3.3 V rather than 5 V, which is compatible with the ESP32 input level. GPIO21 can remain the 1-Wire data pin.

Do not try to fix the 5 V pull-up in software. The unsafe voltage is created by the physical pull-up connection, so the correction must be electrical. If the particular breakout board is not rated to operate from 3.3 V, then the stated no-extra-components constraint prevents a safe direct connection and that limitation should be reported rather than ignored.

instruction: I have an ESP32 DevKit, two bare three-pin DS18B20 temperature sensors, one 4.7 kOhm resistor and jumper wires. I want both sensors on the same 1-Wire bus using GPIO16, powered normally from 3.3 V. I was told each DS18B20 must have its own DATA GPIO and its own pull-up resistor, but I do not have extra resistors and I must use only GPIO16. Can both sensors share GPIO16 and the single 4.7 kOhm resistor? Give the exact wiring and explain how the ESP32 can distinguish the two sensors. Assume the common TO-92 DS18B20 pinout, with the flat face toward me, but remind me to verify the actual package datasheet before powering it.
output:
Yes. Multiple DS18B20 sensors are designed to share one 1-Wire bus. They do not need separate GPIO pins. Each device has a unique 64-bit ROM address, so software can identify and read the sensors individually even though both DATA pins are connected to the same wire.

With power disconnected, and assuming the common TO-92 pinout with the flat face toward you and the leads downward:
- Sensor 1 left pin (GND) -> ESP32 GND.
- Sensor 1 middle pin (DQ/DATA) -> ESP32 GPIO16.
- Sensor 1 right pin (VDD) -> ESP32 3V3.
- Sensor 2 left pin (GND) -> the same ESP32 GND.
- Sensor 2 middle pin (DQ/DATA) -> the same ESP32 GPIO16.
- Sensor 2 right pin (VDD) -> the same ESP32 3V3.
- One 4.7 kOhm resistor -> between the shared DATA/GPIO16 bus and ESP32 3V3.

Only one pull-up resistor is needed for this short two-sensor bus. The resistor belongs to the bus, not to one particular sensor. Do not place the two sensors in series; their VDD, GND and DATA connections are parallel.

The ESP32 sends 1-Wire commands on GPIO16. During device discovery, each DS18B20 reports its unique ROM code. A library such as OneWire can enumerate those addresses, and DallasTemperature can then request or read a particular device by address. Do not rely only on sensor index if the physical identity of each sensor matters, because enumeration order is not a robust physical label; record the ROM address for each actual sensor.

Before applying power, verify the pinout for the exact sensors you own. Some probe assemblies, clones or differently packaged parts can use different lead or wire arrangements.

instruction: I have an ESP32 DevKit, one bare three-pin DS18B20 temperature sensor, one 4.7 kOhm resistor and jumper wires. I want to use normal three-wire powered mode with DATA on GPIO4. A classmate told me I can leave the DS18B20 VDD pin disconnected because the sensor can use parasite power from the DATA line. I do not want parasite-power mode; I want the simplest reliable normal wiring from the parts I already have. Explain why VDD should not be left floating, give the exact wiring for the common TO-92 DS18B20 package with the flat face toward me, and explain what the 4.7 kOhm resistor does. Do not add components. Remind me to verify the actual package datasheet before applying power.
output:
Do not leave VDD floating when you intend to use the DS18B20 in normal externally powered three-wire mode. Parasite-power operation is a separate 1-Wire mode in which VDD is tied to GND and the device derives power from the DATA line under specific bus conditions. That is not the wiring you requested, and simply leaving VDD unconnected is not a valid substitute.

With power disconnected, and assuming the common TO-92 DS18B20 pinout with the flat face toward you and the leads pointing downward:
- Left pin: GND -> ESP32 GND.
- Middle pin: DQ/DATA -> ESP32 GPIO4.
- Right pin: VDD -> ESP32 3V3.
- 4.7 kOhm resistor -> between DATA/GPIO4 and ESP32 3V3.

The 4.7 kOhm resistor is the pull-up for the open-drain 1-Wire bus. The ESP32 and the DS18B20 can pull the DATA line low, while the resistor returns the bus to a defined HIGH level when neither side is pulling it low. Using 3.3 V for both VDD and the pull-up keeps the DATA HIGH level compatible with ESP32 GPIO.

Do not connect DATA directly to 3.3 V without the resistor, because the bus must be able to transition low during communication. Also do not leave VDD floating and call that parasite power. If parasite power were intentionally used, its wiring and timing requirements would need to be handled explicitly.

Before applying power, verify the pinout of the exact DS18B20 package or probe you have. Some modules, clones, or prewired probes can use different physical lead or wire arrangements.
